title: The warehouse with 1.2 million artworks nobody can see
hook: There's a building in Geneva holding more art than most museums. It isn't open to the public, and the paintings in it are, legally, nowhere.
beats: A painting is sold for millions, then disappears into a grey warehouse by the airport.
Inside a freeport, goods count as outside the country, so no import tax until they leave.
Some works are bought, sold and resold without ever moving a metre.
An estimated 1.2 million artworks, about $100 billion, sit there. Nobody publishes the real count.
visuals: Paper paintings sliding into a cut-out vault; customs stamps bouncing off the walls; a tiny collector carrying a key bigger than himself.
ukeepMoment: Ends on: the most valuable things are the ones you can find again. Card collage turns into one searchable list.
check: 1.2 million is a press estimate (Connaissance des Arts), not an official figure. Say "estimated".

title: Why two-thirds of America's biggest companies 'live' in a tiny state
hook: Most of the Fortune 500 have never had an office in Delaware. Legally, that's where they live.
beats: A small state with fewer people than many cities.
About 68% of Fortune 500 companies are incorporated there.
The real draw is its business court and a century of company law, not only tax.
Delaware doesn't tax company income earned outside the state.
visuals: Giant paper office towers squeezed into a tiny paper state; a judge cut-out in a robe stamping documents at speed.
ukeepMoment: Ends on: where a company is registered and where its relationships are are two different maps.

sources.label: CNBC: why more than 60% incorporate in Delaware

check: Use the state's own figure (about 68%) and say so.

title: The €13 billion tax bill Ireland didn't want
hook: In 2024 Europe's top court told Ireland to collect €13 billion from Apple. Ireland had fought for eight years not to.
beats: 2016: the European Commission says Ireland gave Apple an illegal tax deal.
Ireland and Apple both appeal, and win in 2020.
10 September 2024: the Court of Justice overturns that, final, no appeal.
The money had sat in escrow since 2018.
visuals: An apple-shaped money bag on a seesaw between Dublin and Brussels; paper gavels; a vault labelled 'escrow' slowly filling.
ukeepMoment: Keep uKeep out of this one, or use it only in the caption. It's a pure curiosity video that grows the account.
check: Give both sides: Apple said it already paid US tax on those profits.

title: How bored passengers at a tiny Irish airport invented duty free
hook: Every airport in the world has a duty-free shop because of one refuelling stop in the west of Ireland.
beats: Transatlantic planes had to stop at Shannon to refuel.
Brendan O'Regan noticed passengers waiting with nothing to do.
1947: a kiosk of a few square metres opens. The first airport duty free.
Liquor and cigarettes arrive in 1951. Today it's a global industry.
visuals: Paper propeller plane landing; tiny passengers yawning; a kiosk unfolding like a pop-up book into a giant mall.
ukeepMoment: Ends on: big businesses start from noticing people. Who did you notice this week?

sources.label: Business Traveller: 1947, the birth of duty free

check: Most sources say 1947; one headline says the idea came in 1950. Say "the late 1940s" if unsure.

title: From 19 companies in the desert to 11,000
hook: In 1985, Dubai built a free zone next to a port and 19 companies moved in. Today it hosts about 11,000.
beats: The bet: a zone where foreign companies could own 100% and pay no tax.
Today about 10,700 to 11,000 businesses, including 100+ Fortune Global 500 names.
Why it worked: one port, one airport, one time zone between Europe and Asia.
visuals: Sand dunes unfolding into rows of paper warehouses; container ships stacking up; a counter ticking from 19 to 11,000.
ukeepMoment: Ends on Big 5 or GITEX, the shows those companies exhibit at. Your audience's own world.
check: Jafza's own site says 10,700+; a 2026 DP World release says 11,000+. Say "about 11,000".

title: Sending money across the world without moving any money
hook: You hand cash to a man in Dubai. An hour later your family collects it in another country. No money crossed the border.
beats: Two brokers who trust each other, one in each country.
You pay one; the other pays your family from his own cash.
They settle later, sometimes in goods or services.
No contract. If a broker cheats once, nobody deals with him again.
visuals: Two paper figures shaking hands across a map; coins staying put while a dotted line moves; a ledger book with handwritten entries.
ukeepMoment: Ends on: whole systems run on knowing who you can trust. Remember the people you meet.
check: Mention that it's regulated today and can be misused. Don't present it as a how-to.

title: The napkin that bought Messi
hook: Barcelona's first deal with a 13-year-old Messi was written on a paper napkin. In 2024 that napkin sold for £762,400.
beats: 14 December 2000: Messi's family is losing patience with Barcelona.
Sporting director Carles Rexach grabs a napkin and writes a promise to sign him.
The club confirms it properly the same night.
May 2024: Bonhams auctions the napkin for £762,400.
visuals: Restaurant table seen from above; a paper napkin unfolding; a pen scribbling; the napkin flying into an auction house.
ukeepMoment: Ends on: the most important deals start as a quick note. Write it down before it's gone.
check: Use the pound figure; dollar figures vary with the exchange rate.

title: Million-dollar diamond deals with no contract
hook: In the diamond trade, millions change hands on two words and a handshake.
beats: Dealers close with "mazal u'bracha": luck and blessing.
Once said, the deal stands. No lawyers, no signatures.
The enforcement is reputation: break your word once, and nobody trades with you again.
The custom goes back at least to Amsterdam's diamond exchange.
visuals: Close-up paper hands shaking; a loupe zooming into a diamond; a crowd of tiny dealers turning their backs on one figure.
ukeepMoment: Ends on: your network is your contract. Know who you shook hands with.

sources.label: Europa Star: two words worth a contract

check: Origins are disputed. Say "for centuries", not a specific date.

title: The summer camp where billionaires buy newspapers
hook: Jeff Bezos agreed to buy the Washington Post at a summer retreat in Idaho. The price took one sentence.
beats: Every July, Allen & Co. invites media and tech bosses to Sun Valley, Idaho.
2013: Bezos and Don Graham meet there twice.
Graham: "I named a price and Jeff agreed to pay it." $250 million.
Other big media deals have been linked to the same week.
visuals: Private jets parking in rows on a paper runway; fleece vests; two cut-out figures on a bench with a speech bubble showing $250M.
ukeepMoment: Ends on: the biggest deals happen where people meet in person. And then someone has to follow up.

sources.label: Fortune: classic deals of Sun Valley

check: They had talked earlier in 2013. Say the deal was agreed there, not that they first met there.

title: Why Tupperware vanished from stores and sold better
hook: In 1951, Tupperware pulled its products out of every shop. Sales went up.
beats: Plastic boxes with a strange 'burp' lid sat unsold on store shelves.
Brownie Wise was selling them at parties in people's living rooms.
Earl Tupper copies her: stores out, home parties in.
She becomes one of the best-known saleswomen in America, until he fires her in 1958.
visuals: Paper shelves with dusty boxes; a living room filling with cut-out guests; lids burping with little speech bubbles.
ukeepMoment: Ends on: people buy from people they've met. The real product is the relationship.
check: She didn't invent home parties; she perfected them. Say it that way.

title: The desk gadget that was worth more than a salary
hook: In the 1980s, people changing jobs fought over one object: their Rolodex.
beats: 1956: a rotating card file is invented for secretaries.
Hollywood puts it on every power desk.
Your Rolodex was your network, and your network was your value.
Then it moved into phones, and most of it got lost.
visuals: Spinning paper card wheel; cards flying out into the shapes of people; a briefcase tug-of-war.
ukeepMoment: The most natural uKeep ending of the bank: the Rolodex never died, it just needs a new home.

sources.label: Cooper Hewitt: the power of the Rolodex

check: Who invented it is disputed (Neustadter or his engineer Hildaur Neilsen). Say "invented in 1956" without naming one.

title: Your next job won't come from a friend
hook: LinkedIn ran an experiment on 20 million people. New jobs came most often from acquaintances, not close friends.
beats: 1973: sociologist Mark Granovetter's idea, the strength of weak ties.
2022: LinkedIn tests it over five years, 600,000 new jobs.
The sweet spot: people you know a little and rarely talk to.
Close friends know what you know. Acquaintances know what you don't.
visuals: A web of paper people; thick strings to friends, thin threads to acquaintances; a job offer travelling along the thinnest thread.
ukeepMoment: Ends on: weak ties are the ones you forget first. The person from one conference, met once.
check: The effect is an inverted U: moderately weak ties help most, not the weakest. Keep that nuance.

title: You're 3.57 people away from anyone
hook: It's not six degrees of separation any more. Facebook measured it: 3.57.
beats: 1960s: Milgram's letters experiment gives us 'six degrees'.
2016: Facebook measures 1.6 billion accounts: 3.57 people between any two.
In the US it's 3.46.
Which means someone you met last month is probably two steps from your next big customer.
visuals: A paper letter hopping hand to hand across a map; the chain shrinking from 6 links to 3.5.
ukeepMoment: Ends on: the chain only works if you remember the links.
check: It covers Facebook users only, not everyone. Say "between Facebook users".

title: Your brain can only hold about 150 relationships. Maybe.
hook: A scientist says your brain caps your real relationships at about 150. Other scientists say that's nonsense.
beats: Dunbar compares primate brain size and group size and predicts about 150 for humans.
He finds it in Christmas card lists, villages, army units.
2021: a Stockholm team reruns the maths and gets anywhere from 2 to 520.
The fight is still open. What's clear: you can't keep up with everyone without help.
visuals: A paper brain with 150 tiny portraits pinned inside; a second brain where the portraits spill out; two scientists throwing graphs.
ukeepMoment: Ends on: whatever the number, the rest of the people you meet need to be written down somewhere.

sources.label: The Conversation: why we dispute it

check: Show both sides. The debate is the hook.

title: Why the world's biggest tech show is in a gambling city
hook: Las Vegas has about 151,000 hotel rooms. From Sunday to Thursday, tourists don't fill them. Trade shows do.
beats: Weekends belong to tourists; weekdays used to be empty.
Conventions fill the midweek gap, and their visitors spend more.
CES alone has brought nearly 5 million visitors over the decades.
2021, when CES went virtual: January room rates collapsed.
visuals: A paper hotel tower with lights switching on floor by floor as badges arrive; a calendar flipping Sun–Thu; prices dropping like dice.
ukeepMoment: Ends on: tens of thousands of business cards change hands in one week. Where do they all go?

sources.label: CDC Gaming Reports: conventions fill hotels midweek

check: Figures come from different years. Don't add them up.

title: How a tuberculosis town became the world's most exclusive meeting
hook: Before world leaders came to Davos, it was where people came to cure tuberculosis.
beats: The 1800s: patients come for the thin, dry mountain air.
Thomas Mann sets The Magic Mountain in a Davos sanatorium.
Antibiotics empty the clinics. 1971: a professor invites about 450 European executives.
It becomes the World Economic Forum in 1987.
visuals: Paper mountain; patients on balconies wrapped in blankets; the same balconies refilling with suits and lanyards.
ukeepMoment: Ends on: the meeting is the easy part. What happens with the people you met there?
check: Attendance in 1971 is given as 400–450. Say "about 450".

title: The trade fair that occupying soldiers started in a factory
hook: The world's biggest industrial fair was started in 1947 by a foreign army, in bombed-out factory halls.
beats: Germany's traditional fair city, Leipzig, is in the Soviet zone.
The British military government wants exports to restart in its zone.
August 1947: an export fair opens in factory halls near Hanover.
736,000 visitors from 53 countries, about $32 million in deals.
visuals: A paper map split in two; trucks rolling into a half-ruined hall; order books filling up page by page.
ukeepMoment: Ends on: trade shows exist so strangers can meet and do business. Then the follow-up begins.
check: Use Deutsche Messe's own visitor and deal figures.

title: From 1,223 buyers to a fair you can't see in a week
hook: In 1957, China's Canton Fair had 1,223 foreign buyers. Today it has more booths than some towns have houses.
beats: 1957: about 9,600 m² in Guangzhou, 19 countries.
It runs twice a year, without stopping, for almost 70 years.
2025: around 74,000 booths and about 31,000 exhibitors.
Buyers fly in to find factories in person.
visuals: A single paper stall multiplying into an endless grid; a tiny buyer with a giant map; stacks of cards rising like skyscrapers.
ukeepMoment: Ends on: how many business cards does one buyer bring home from that? (Show a suitcase bursting.)
check: Call it China's largest trade fair. "World's largest" isn't confirmed.
